output.myth: Ennu the Kite-Wright made the first black-tailed kite from old sailcloth and a hank of ewe's wool dyed in soot. Nobody asked him why. He said grief is heavy and wants something to hold it down. So on the morning after a death, the family climbs to the cliff edge with the kite and ties the black tail to the cord, so the dead can see the way up to Vel. Hesk counts every one as it climbs. Tavo the Gale once tore a black kite from a widow's hands and laughed until the rocks rang, and she had to let it go. Aun flew the first one he was sorry for, and it went up and never came down. Our hands are still on the string, and the wool still smells of smoke. Fly it at dawn. Vel is not far, only cold.
output.verse:
Black wool on her tail,
the dead lift up through the wind,
Vel is open now.
